question: What is the minimum total contribution into a workplace pension under automatic enrolment, and how much of it must the employer pay?
reference_answer: At least 8% of your earnings in total, of which the employer must pay at least 3%.

question: How is tax relief added under relief at source?
reference_answer: The pension provider claims tax relief from the government at the basic 20% rate and adds it to the pension pot.

question: What is the annual allowance for pension savings this tax year?
reference_answer: £60,000 this tax year; you only pay tax if you go above it.

question: How many National Insurance qualifying years do I need to get any new State Pension?
reference_answer: At least 10 qualifying years.

question: how much is the full new state pension a week?
reference_answer: The full rate of the new State Pension is £241.30 a week. Your own amount depends on your National Insurance record, so it could be different.

question: My National Insurance record only started in 2018. How many qualifying years do I need for the full new State Pension?
reference_answer: 35 qualifying years, because your National Insurance record started after April 2016.

question: Does the State Pension go up every year? By how much?
reference_answer: Yes. The new State Pension rises each year by whichever is highest: average growth in wages, growth in prices measured by the Consumer Prices Index (CPI), or 2.5%.

question: I'm a woman born in May 1952. Will I get the new State Pension?
reference_answer: No. The new State Pension is for women born on or after 6 April 1953. If you were born before then, you get the basic State Pension instead, and you may also get Additional State Pension.

question: Do I have to stop working once I reach State Pension age?
reference_answer: No. You can keep working after you reach State Pension age; the default retirement age (a forced retirement age of 65) no longer exists.

question: What happens if I just put off claiming my State Pension when I reach the age?
reference_answer: It is deferred automatically and you don't have to do anything. When you do claim, you can usually take what you deferred as a one-off payment or as increased regular payments, called 'extra State Pension'. Extra payments from deferring could be taxed.

question: I'm self-employed and only make about £6,000 profit a year. Is that a reason people pay voluntary National Insurance?
reference_answer: Yes. Being self-employed with annual profits of less than £7,105 is one of the reasons the guidance gives for paying voluntary contributions.

question: I'm not earning anything at the moment. How much can I pay into a pension each year and still get tax relief?
reference_answer: Up to £2,880 a tax year (6 April to 5 April). If you have no earnings, a pension provider using relief at source can claim tax relief for you at 20% on contributions up to that amount.

question: I pay 40% tax and my pension uses relief at source. Do I get all my tax relief automatically?
reference_answer: No. Your provider claims the first 20% for you. You claim the extra 20% (on income you paid 40% tax on) yourself, through your Self Assessment tax return, or another way if you don't file one.

question: Can I pay for life insurance out of my pension contributions and still get tax relief?
reference_answer: Not for a personal term assurance policy, unless it is a protected policy.

question: Will I have to pay tax on my State Pension?
reference_answer: You pay tax if your total annual income, which can include the State Pension, adds up to more than your Personal Allowance.

question: I didn't use all my annual allowance in previous years. Can I carry it over?
reference_answer: If you use all of this tax year's annual allowance, you might be able to carry over unused allowance from the previous 3 tax years.

question: I'm on a high income. When does my annual allowance get tapered?
reference_answer: You get a reduced ('tapered') annual allowance in the current tax year if your threshold income is over £200,000 and your adjusted income is over £260,000.

question: My dad had to retire early through serious ill health and took all his pension pots. Will he be taxed for going over the annual allowance?
reference_answer: No. HMRC does not tax anyone for going over their annual allowance in a tax year if they retired and took all their pension pots because of serious ill health.

question: How much tax-free cash can I take from my pension?
reference_answer: You can usually take up to 25% of the amount built up in a pension as a tax-free lump sum, up to a maximum of £268,275. A protected allowance may let you take more.

question: What's the earliest I can usually take money out of my workplace pension?
reference_answer: Usually 55 at the earliest. Most schemes set an age when you can take your pension, usually between 60 and 65, and the scheme's rules decide.

question: A company says it can get cash out of my pension before I turn 55. Is there a catch?
reference_answer: Taking your pension early in this way could mean you pay tax of up to 55%.

question: I opted into my work pension myself. Does my employer have to put anything in?
reference_answer: Yes, if you earn more than £520 a month, £120 a week or £480 over 4 weeks, your employer must contribute the minimum amount. If you earn those amounts or less, they don't have to contribute anything.

question: Which part of my pay are my workplace pension contributions based on?
reference_answer: In most automatic enrolment schemes, on your total earnings between £6,240 and £50,270 a year before tax. Total earnings include salary or wages, bonuses and commission, overtime and statutory payments such as sick or maternity pay.

question: What's the phone number for the Pension Tracing Service?
reference_answer: 0800 731 0175, or +44 (0)191 218 7777 from outside the UK. Lines are open Monday to Friday, 10am to 3pm.

question: I'm on Pension Credit. Do I get a free TV licence?
reference_answer: Yes, if you're aged 75 or over.

question: I've been auto-enrolled. What's the minimum my employer and I each have to pay, and is it worked out on all of my pay?
reference_answer: The total minimum is 8%: your employer pays at least 3% and you pay 5%, and scheme rules can make these higher. In some schemes your employer pays more than the legal minimum, and then you can pay less as long as the 8% total is met. In most automatic enrolment schemes it is worked out on your total earnings between £6,240 and £50,270 a year before tax, not on all of your pay.

question: How many years of National Insurance do I need to get any State Pension, and how many for the full amount?
reference_answer: You need at least 10 qualifying years to get any new State Pension. For the full rate you need 35 qualifying years if your record started after April 2016, and usually more than 35 if you were contracted out before then.

question: What's the most I can pay into my pensions each year with tax relief, and what's the annual allowance?
reference_answer: You can get tax relief on contributions worth up to 100% of your annual earnings. The annual allowance is £60,000 this tax year; you pay tax on pension savings above it.

question: How much can I take tax-free when I take my pension, and what happens if I take a bigger lump sum?
reference_answer: You can usually take up to 25% tax-free, up to £268,275. You pay Income Tax on any part of a lump sum above your lump sum allowance (or your lump sum and death benefit allowance), and if you take a small pot all as a lump sum, 25% is tax-free and you pay Income Tax on the rest. Taking a large amount may mean paying a higher rate of tax.

question: If I retire at 60, can I get my State Pension straight away? And what about my workplace pension?
reference_answer: The earliest you can get your State Pension is your State Pension age, so if you retire before then you have to wait to claim it. A workplace pension depends on the scheme: most set an age between 60 and 65, and the earliest is usually 55.

question: If I put off claiming my State Pension, will the extra be taxed? And when do I pay tax on pension income anyway?
reference_answer: Extra payments you get from deferring could be taxed. You pay tax when your total annual income, including the State Pension and any private pension, adds up to more than your Personal Allowance.

question: I've lost track of an old workplace pension. How do I find it, and what do I need to know first?
reference_answer: The Pension Tracing Service can help. You can use the online service to find contact details, or ask the Pension Tracing Service by phone or post. You need the name of an employer or a pension provider, and it won't tell you whether you have a pension or what it's worth.

question: What is Pension Credit, and what other help can I get if I'm on it?
reference_answer: Pension Credit gives you extra money for living costs if you're over State Pension age and on a low income, and can help with housing costs. With it you can also get other help, such as Housing Benefit if you rent, Cold Weather Payments, a Council Tax Reduction and a free TV licence if you're 75 or over.

question: What investment return did the average workplace pension fund make last year?
reference_answer: Not covered by the guidance.

question: How much Pension Credit would I get a week if I live on my own?
reference_answer: Not covered by the guidance: it explains what Pension Credit is but gives no amounts.

question: How much is the lump sum and death benefit allowance?
reference_answer: Not covered by the guidance: it names the lump sum and death benefit allowance but gives no figure.

question: What's the Personal Allowance this tax year, in pounds?
reference_answer: Not covered by the guidance: it says you pay tax on income above your Personal Allowance but doesn't give the amount.

question: How much does it cost to pay one year of voluntary National Insurance?
reference_answer: Not covered by the guidance: it says to check your National Insurance record to find out the cost, but gives no figure.

question: How much extra State Pension do I get for every week I put off claiming it?
reference_answer: Not covered by the guidance: it says what you get depends on when you reach State Pension age, but gives no rate.

question: What tax code will my pension provider put me on?
reference_answer: Not covered by the guidance.

question: What's the cap on charges for a stakeholder pension?
reference_answer: Not covered by the guidance: it says stakeholder pensions have limits on charges but doesn't give them.

question: How much is the Additional State Pension worth a week?
reference_answer: Not covered by the guidance.

question: How much is the Winter Fuel Payment this year?
reference_answer: Not covered by the guidance.

question: What's a final salary pension?
reference_answer: Another name for a defined benefit pension (also called career average). It's usually a workplace pension arranged by your employer, and what you get depends on the scheme's rules, for example your salary and how long you've worked for your employer, not on investments or how much you've paid in.

question: What's the least my employer has to put in under auto-enrolment?
reference_answer: Under automatic enrolment the minimum employer contribution is 3%, within a total minimum contribution of 8%.

question: How is a DB pension worked out?
reference_answer: A DB (defined benefit) pension depends on the scheme's rules, not on investments or how much was paid in. Workplace schemes usually base it on things like your salary and how long you've worked for your employer, and the provider promises a certain amount each year when you retire.

question: what is a money purchase pension
reference_answer: Another name for a defined contribution pension: a pot based on how much is paid in, which the provider invests, so its value can go up or down.

question: What is the MPAA?
reference_answer: The money purchase annual allowance: a lower annual allowance that can apply if you flexibly access your pension, for example by taking cash from your pension pot.

question: What's a SIPP?
reference_answer: A self-invested personal pension: a type of personal pension that lets you control the specific investments that make up your pension fund.

question: What's an occupational pension?
reference_answer: Another name for a workplace pension: a way of saving for your retirement that's arranged by your employer.

question: Should I move my defined benefit pension into a personal pension?
reference_answer: The guidance doesn't say what you should do. It lists reasons people move a pension, and says you can get free, impartial information about transferring from MoneyHelper, or impartial advice about workplace pensions from an independent financial adviser, which you usually pay for.

question: Should I pay voluntary National Insurance to fill the gaps in my record?
reference_answer: The guidance doesn't decide for you. It says voluntary contributions don't always increase your State Pension, for example if you were contracted out, and to check whether you're eligible for National Insurance credits before deciding to pay. To find out if you'd benefit, check your National Insurance record and State Pension forecast or contact the Future Pension Centre if you're below State Pension age, or contact the Pension Service if you've reached it.

question: Should I delay my State Pension or start taking it straight away?
reference_answer: The guidance doesn't recommend either. It explains that an unclaimed State Pension is deferred automatically and can later be taken as a one-off payment or as higher regular payments, and that the extra could be taxed.

question: Should I take my 25% tax-free lump sum now?
reference_answer: The guidance doesn't say whether you should. It explains that you can usually take up to 25% tax-free, up to £268,275, and that you pay Income Tax on any part of a lump sum above your lump sum allowance.

question: I'd rather have more take-home pay. Should I opt out of my workplace pension?
reference_answer: The guidance doesn't advise on this. It says joining reduces your take-home pay but may mean you're entitled to an income-related benefit or make smaller student loan repayments, and that in most cases your employer also pays in.

question: What will the annual allowance be in the 2030 to 2031 tax year?
reference_answer: Not covered by the guidance: it gives only this tax year's annual allowance (£60,000), not future years.

question: How much was the full new State Pension a week last year?
reference_answer: Not covered by the guidance: it gives the full rate of the new State Pension as £241.30 a week, but no figures for earlier years.

question: What's the minimum I have to pay into a personal pension I set up myself?
reference_answer: Not covered by the guidance: its minimum contributions (5% from you, 8% in total) are for automatic enrolment workplace pensions, not personal pensions you arrange yourself.

question: Is the earliest age I can take my pension going up to 57?
reference_answer: Not covered by the guidance: it says the earliest is usually 55 and doesn't mention any change.

question: What's the lowest my annual allowance can be tapered down to?
reference_answer: Not covered by the guidance: it says when the tapered allowance applies (threshold income over £200,000 and adjusted income over £260,000), but not how low it can go.
